Ahio
uh-HYE-oh
proper noun
Hebrew Achyo, “brotherly” or “his brother,” a son of Abinadab who drove the cart bearing the ark.

📖 Biblical Definition

Ahio was a son of Abinadab, the brother of Uzzah, who together drove the new cart on which the ark of God was carried up from his father’s house in Gibeah toward Jerusalem (2Sa 6:3). “Ahio went before the ark” while Uzzah walked beside it (2Sa 6:4). But the journey ended in sorrow, for the oxen stumbled at the threshingfloor of Nachon, and Uzzah put forth his hand to steady the ark, and the LORD smote him that he died, because the ark had been carried in a way the LORD had not commanded. The ark was meant to be borne upon the shoulders of the Levites by its staves, not drawn upon a cart after the manner of the Philistines; and the careless handling of the holy thing, however well-intended, brought death. Ahio, who went before the ark, is a quiet figure in this solemn scene. His brief appearance is bound up with the great lesson of Uzzah’s death: that God must be approached and served in the way He has appointed, not after the inventions of men. Ahio witnesses, with his brother, that good intentions do not excuse disobedience in the worship of God, and that the holy must be handled with holy fear.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A son of Abinadab who, with his brother Uzzah, drove the cart bearing the ark; he went before it.

expand to see more

AHIO, a son of Abinadab, the brother of Uzzah.

He and Uzzah drove the new cart bearing the ark from Gibeah (2Sa 6:3).

Ahio went before the ark on the way (2Sa 6:4).

The journey ended when Uzzah was smitten for touching the ark.

His scene teaches that the ark was to be borne by the Levites, not on a cart.

📖 Key Scripture

2Sa 6:3 — "And they set the ark of God upon a new cart, and brought it out of the house of Abinadab that was in Gibeah: and Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, drave the new cart."

2Sa 6:4 — "And they brought it out of the house of Abinadab which was at Gibeah, accompanying the ark of God: and Ahio went before the ark."

2Sa 6:6 — "And when they came to Nachon's threshingfloor, Uzzah put forth his hand to the ark of God, and took hold of it; for the oxen shook it."

1Ch 15:13 — "For because ye did it not at the first, the LORD our God made a breach upon us, for that we sought him not after the due order."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; his scene teaches that God must be served in the way He appoints.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the lesson of the cart and the threshingfloor: the ark was to be borne upon the shoulders of the Levites by its staves, as God commanded, not drawn upon a new cart after the manner of the Philistines. Ahio and Uzzah meant well, but they served God in a way He had not appointed, and Uzzah died. Good intentions do not sanctify disobedience; the LORD is to be worshipped after His own due order, not the inventions of men.

This solemn scene is one of the clearest Old Testament witnesses to the regulative principle of worship: that what God has commanded is required, and what He has not commanded is not to be added by human will. David himself later confessed, “we sought him not after the due order” (1Ch 15:13). The worship of God is His to define; reverent obedience, not creative innovation, is what He requires of His people.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name means “brotherly” or “his brother,” borne by this son of Abinadab.

Ahio — Hebrew Achyo, “brotherly” or “his brother.”

The element ach means “brother.”

He was a son of Abinadab, the brother of Uzzah.

He went before the ark as it was drawn on the cart.

His scene is bound up with the death of Uzzah.

Usage

"Like Ahio at the cart, men may serve God with good intent yet in a way He has not appointed."

"Ahio teaches that the LORD is to be worshipped after His own due order, not human invention."

"The cart and the threshingfloor witness that good intentions do not sanctify disobedience."
